item.title: Entanglement percolation enhanced by the power of choice
item.description: arXiv:2611.10119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum communication networks are best supported by maximally entangled states, but imperfections in entanglement generation and distribution generally limit the distributed states to being only partially entangled. Therefore, protocols typically consisting of local operations and classical communication are required to create suitably entangled networks. Here, we introduce a power-of-choice (PoC) protocol based on reversing the selection criteria in the Achlioptas process previously considered in classical explosive percolation. The resulting PoC protocol anticipates the entanglement percolation transition, thereby reducing the entanglement resources needed to establish quantum communication. Notably, in contrast to explosive percolation, the PoC protocol admits an implementation using local information with no appreciable loss of performance.
item.dc:creator: Yanxuan Shao, Adilson E. Motter

item.title: Bayes-Optimal Quantum Computational Sensing via Convex Spectral Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.10146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computational sensing performs task-specific inference directly through coherent sensing dynamics, avoiding an intermediate estimation step. Existing designs, however, typically optimize quantum control parameters through nonconvex programs whose performance can depend strongly on initialization. This contribution formulates binary phase classification directly in terms of the sensor's measurement response. For a fixed query budget, generalized quantum signal processing (GQSP) restricts this response to a bounded trigonometric polynomial, while the Bayes classification error is linear in the response. These properties yield an exact finite-dimensional semidefinite program for the globally Bayes-optimal sensor response. Fej\'er--Riesz factorization and GQSP synthesis then recover a physically realizable control sequence. The same formulation extends naturally to sample-based design and additive phase uncertainty. Numerical tests show improved accuracy and optimization reliability over direct control-angle training; noise-aware redesign also lowers error under phase uncertainty.
item.dc:creator: Amirhossein Taherpour, Alireza Sadeghi, Georgios B. Giannakis

item.title: Symplectic Reck: In-Situ Learning of Gaussian Quantum Operations
item.description: arXiv:2611.10206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Programmable photonic circuits are a natural platform for physical learning, where hardware parameters are trained directly from measured feedback. We propose a physical learning algorithm and architecture for continuous-variable quantum systems where a photonic circuit is trained in situ to invert an unknown lossless Gaussian quantum operation. We prove that a generic symplectic matrix $S\in\mathrm{Sp}(2N,\mathbb{R})$ admits a decomposition into a triangular array of two-mode symplectic gates on neighboring modes, followed by single-mode symplectic gates. We then introduce the symplectic Reck mesh, which physically realizes this factorization, generalizing the unitary Reck mesh widely used in optical neural networks. When placed after an unknown Gaussian unitary, the mesh is trained in situ by nulling local response blocks one at a time using optical probes and measurements. We identify a local condition number that quantifies the squeezing required for a nulling step and its sensitivity to measurement error. We numerically demonstrate finite-shot training and robustness to systematic gate-calibration errors. Our work extends self-configuring optical networks from unitary to symplectic transformations, bringing physical learning to continuous-variable quantum photonic hardware.
item.dc:creator: Janet F. Zhong, Renwen Yu, Paul-Alexis Mor, Charles Roques-Carmes, Aviv Karnieli, David A. B. Miller, Shanhui Fan

item.title: Can One Hear the Size of a Clock?
item.description: arXiv:2611.10252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weyl's law counts the vibration modes that fit into a cavity, and a quantum system with $d$ levels can oscillate at up to $d(d-1)/2$ frequencies without decay. For systems that jump at random between states, no such count was known: they oscillate only out of equilibrium, and the random timing of their jumps damps every oscillation. We find the missing count: if $Q$ is the ratio of frequency to decay rate, a system of $d$ states sustains fewer than $2(d-1)/(\pi Q)$ oscillations whose ratio exceeds $Q$. Nested cycles approach this bound, and measured oscillations reveal how large a hidden system must be.
item.dc:creator: Markus Baumann, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien

item.title: Experimental visual quantum state discrimination
item.description: arXiv:2611.10282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Almost all solutions to vision tasks $\unicode{x2014}$ offered by nature and technology alike $\unicode{x2014}$ rely on capturing an image using a lens or a similar optical instrument, followed by computational analysis by neurons of a brain or a digital computer. This approach is inherently suboptimal in photon-limited and noisy conditions, where critical information is irreversibly lost at the measurement stage. We address this gap by introducing AI-driven optimization of quantum measurements on the incoming photons, learning how to extract the maximum possible information for a given computer vision task from each incoming photon. The trained measurement consists of a diffractive optical neural network (DONN) followed by a detector array. We train the DONN with a quantum information-theoretic objective that maximizes the rate at which the discrimination error decays as photons accumulate. The resulting measurement achieves exponentially lower error than both direct imaging and a DONN optimized for single-photon discrimination. We validate the advantage in a noiseless setting as well as a photon-counting experiment with an electron-multiplying CCD with the noise corresponding to $10^4$ photons per single signal photon, where the measurement also learns to mitigate the detector noise.
item.dc:creator: A. Duplinskiy, M. J. Filipovich, A. I. Lvovsky

item.title: Regev's Reduction Reaches Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2611.10283v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Regev's reduction uses a quantum Fourier transform to carry out reductions between various problems related to lattices and codes. We apply it to the problem of sampling from Gibbs distributions of certain classical spin glass Hamiltonians, which can equivalently be thought of as cost functions for average-case instances of an optimization problem called $D$-regular max-$k$-LINSAT. This problem becomes hard at low temperature. Here, we use a quantum decoding algorithm called Belief Propagation with Quantum Messages (BPQM) to solve the decoding problem arising from Regev's reduction. Our main contribution is a proof that the minimum temperature reachable using Regev+BPQM is exactly equal to the reconstruction threshold temperature for noisy channels transmitting signals on a tree network. This equality can be understood via Renes' duality between classical and quantum channels, which we use to show that quantum decoding is possible exactly when classical reconstruction on the dual problem is impossible. M{\'e}zard and Montanari identified this reconstruction temperature with a dynamical glass transition predicted by the one-step replica-symmetry breaking (1RSB) cavity equation. It is conjectured that local samplers such as Metropolis Monte Carlo and Glauber dynamics cannot equilibrate efficiently below this reconstruction temperature but may do so above it; our large numerical experiments show close agreement with this prediction across hundreds of different problem parameters. Therefore, our results rigorously show that Regev+BPQM reaches a temperature for which, to our knowledge, there is no matching classical guarantee, and brings Regev+BPQM to the conjectured limit of efficient Gibbs sampling by classical local dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Stephen P. Jordan, Quynh T. Nguyen, Leo Zhou

item.title: Practical Ellipse Fitting for Atom Interferometry
item.description: arXiv:2611.10289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In differential atom interferometry, it is necessary to extract the differential phase shift between two interferometers that are individually noisy. A variety of techniques can be used for this purpose, under the general label of ellipse fitting. We compare several methods for ellipse fitting, considering parameters and performance relevant to atom interferometry. Statistical, algebraic, geometric and Bayesian methods are discussed, and we describe a novel "reciprocal" geometric method that offers some benefits. Each method has advantages and disadvantages that depend on the use case required. Supplemental material includes basic Python and Matlab code for each method.
item.dc:creator: N. Fowler, D. B. Reinhardt, M Meister, C. A. Sackett

item.title: Dynamical Light-Matter Coupling with Protected Superconducting Oscillators
item.description: arXiv:2611.10295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Superconducting circuits hosting long-lived bosonic modes are an excellent platform for emulating the dynamics of light and matter and exploiting them for quantum information processing. The space of accessible dynamics is greatly extended by introducing the frequency tunability of artificial atoms, whereby the interactions with the light field of a microwave cavity can be modified on demand. However, using external flux bias to control the frequency of transmons introduces significant losses to coupled cavities, reducing their single-photon lifetimes to a few tens of $\mu$s. These imperfections compromise the usefulness of the bosonic mode, which loses its ability to store and manipulate the quantum information of many-photon states. This thesis investigates the issue and demonstrates how to enhance the flux control of microwave cavities without compromising protection. Several hardware solutions were explored, including off-plane remote flux sources routed by a magnetic hose, and lithographically printed on-chip lines equipped with multiple stages of filtering. These developments equip the systems with broadband flux control and photon lifetimes of several hundred $\mu$s. They enable the real-time manipulation of the two central parameters of the Rabi model: detuning and coupling strength. This flexibility translates into operational primitives of interest, such as the calibration of nonlinearities to different interaction regimes, the activation of parametric resonances with adjustable coupling strengths, and the use of number-selective transmon-cavity transitions for qudit state preparation and control. These results lay the groundwork for exploring richer synthetic light-matter systems, controlling cavities with more complex nonlinear circuits, and engineering driven-dissipative systems with applications in quantum computation and sensing.
item.dc:creator: Fernando Valadares

item.title: Adaptive Protocol for R\'enyi Entropy Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.10330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The second-order R\'enyi entropy is one of the most important quantities used for characterizing the entanglement structure of states prepared in quantum many-body experiments. With access to qubit projective measurement data, it can be estimated via a protocol in which repeated measurements are taken after each of a set of random local unitary operations is applied to the quantum state. To obtain accurate values for the second R\'enyi entropy on shot-limited devices, care must be taken when choosing the number of different unitary settings to apply, and the respective number of projective measurements to take. In this paper, we propose an adaptive protocol for estimating the R\'enyi entropy that iteratively optimizes the ratio of basis settings to measurements, using a gradient-based approach and starting from an initial small set of measurements. Using synthetic data, we demonstrate that for several prototypical states, our method converges to values for this ratio that are comparable to the optimal values obtained by a brute-force grid search, and it exhibits slower growth of the measurement budget required for a fixed target accuracy than fixed-ratio protocols. Our adaptive protocol therefore promotes efficient estimation of the R\'enyi entropy in finite-size, shot-limited quantum experiments by making effective use of the available measurement budget.
item.dc:creator: Mu Niu, Yi Hong Teoh, Roger G. Melko, Rajibul Islam

item.title: Realizing Unstructured PDE Forecasting on Superconducting Quantum Processors
item.description: arXiv:2611.10351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating high dimensional unstructured Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) with quantum processors is a major challenge with significant potential benefit. Existing methods have been demonstrated at small qubit counts, on simplifications of realistic problems. We implement a quantum reservoir network (QRN) for forecasting high-dimensional unstructured PDEs using up to 52 qubits on IBM superconducting hardware. Our method is gradient-free and does not suffer from the challenges of variational quantum algorithms. Instead, the QRN provides a large kernel space, up to 2^52 dimensions and beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, that remains useful under current hardware noise levels. Furthermore, a partial measure-and-reset mechanism enables total circuit runtime for ~24 times the qubit coherence time, so qubit lifetimes do not limit the forecast horizon. Thus, our method enables forecasting realistic unstructured nonlinear PDEs on quantum hardware. Typical difficulties associated with predicting large scale PDEs, such as transpilation, exponential shot requirements, hardware noise, and short qubit lifetimes are mitigated through careful design considerations and a dynamic observable reconstruction method. We validate our approach using a ~34k cell unstructured 2D cylinder flow at Reynolds number 1000 and a challenging nonlinear Gray--Scott reaction--diffusion problem, demonstrating high fidelity prediction on CUDA-Q simulation and on 26 and 52-qubit superconducting quantum processors. Specifically, we show that adding QRN features to an autoencoder linear prediction pipeline reduces prediction error by 21%-43%. Finally, we demonstrate closed-loop autoregressive PDE forecasting on these problems. This work demonstrates, for the first time, quantum circuits with depth beyond qubit lifetimes achieving accurate unstructured mesh forecasting on highly nonlinear PDEs.
item.dc:creator: Erik Connerty, Jonathan Eastridge, Taylor Patti, Gerasimos Angelatos, Ethan N. Evans

item.title: A trace costs one quantifier: the exact complexity of perfect play in nonlocal games
item.description: arXiv:2611.10481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a finite nonlocal game, can the players win with certainty? We prove that the existence of a perfect normal spatial strategy is $\Sigma^0_2$-complete, even when restricted to games of value one, so it cannot be decided even with an oracle for the halting problem. This is strictly harder than perfect play in the finite-dimensional and commuting-operator models, which are $\Sigma^0_1$-complete and $\Pi^0_1$-complete. Within the commuting model, the existence of a perfect normal strategy with a finite or semifinite von Neumann host is $\Sigma^0_2$-complete, whereas for every fixed type $\mathrm{III}_\lambda$ subtype it has the same $\Pi^0_1$-complete language as unrestricted commuting play. A trace thus costs one existential number quantifier: the hardness constructions force every perfect strategy to choose a finite clock period or a finite tree depth. Spatial $\Sigma^0_2$-completeness also holds when finite entanglement entropy is required, and both forms are formally verified in Lean. For every computable $0<\alpha<1$, perfect spatial play with $\mathrm{Tr}\,h^\alpha<\infty$ for the reduced density $h$ is $\Sigma^0_2$-complete as well; these conditions form a strict ladder between finite rank and finite entropy. We also prove $\Sigma^0_2$-completeness for one-shot zero-error communication with normal entanglement, and construct a finite channel with zero-error codes of a given size each of which needs infinite entanglement entropy.
item.dc:creator: Seth Douglas, Nidhal Mghirbi

item.title: On the estimation of linear-optical amplitudes and probabilities with entangled input state
item.description: arXiv:2611.10500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most proposed applications of boson samplers, including photonic machine-learning models, do not use the samples themselves but estimates of output probabilities, marginals or overlaps, obtained to additive precision from a finite number of shots. For product inputs such as single photons, these quantities can already be estimated classically with Gurvits's algorithm and its generalisations. We ask whether entangled inputs change this picture. For any $n$-photon input that is a matrix-product state of bond dimension $\chi$, with one photon per site and $L$ modes per site, we give an unbiased estimator of any output amplitude of an $m$-mode interferometer, whose mean-square error after $N$ draws is at most $\|\psi\|^2/N$ whatever the interferometer, the output pattern and the entanglement of the state. Each draw costs $O(nL\chi^2+nL^3+mn)$ operations after $O(nL\chi^3)$ preprocessing, and an additive error $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$ requires $O(\|\psi\|^2\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$ draws, with memory of the order of the input size. The main application is to light emitted sequentially by quantum emitters, such as spin-based sources of photonic cluster states, for which $\chi$ is bounded by the dimension of the source's retained quantum memory: one spin gives $\chi=2$ at any length, and a memory of $k$ qubits, held in emitters or in photons stored in a delay line, gives $\chi\le2^k$, so the cost stays polynomial as long as $k=O(\log n)$. The same sampler also estimates traced-memory probabilities, overlaps and individual marginal probabilities. All guarantees are additive: the estimator gives neither relative estimates of exponentially small probabilities nor a sampler of the output distribution.
item.dc:creator: Jean Senellart, Pierre-Emmanuel Emeriau

item.title: Delta-Corrected Shot Reduction for Bypassing Optimization Plateaus in Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
item.description: arXiv:2611.10524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) remains a cornerstone hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for quantum simulation, yet its scalability is fundamentally constrained by heavy measurement overheads. While strategies such as variance-preserved shot reduction (VPSR) mitigates this cost, they suffer from convergence instability and optimization stagnation caused by finite-sample bias in limited pilot shots. To overcome this limitation, we introduce delta-corrected shot reduction (DCSR), an analytically enhanced shot allocation strategy that rigorously mitigates finite-sample instability. Utilizing the multivariate delta method, we derive explicit higher-order bias correction terms for the empirical reduction factor. Both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations reveal that incorporating higher-order statistical moments, such as skewness and kurtosis, provides the gradient resolution necessary to bypass noise-induced barren plateaus. DSCR significantly accelerates convergence compared to standard VPSR across diverse noise and resource regimes while matching or decreasing cumulative measurement costs, establishing a mathematically rigorous framework for variance-stabilized shot allocation on near-term hardware.
item.dc:creator: Jamie Evander Ghozaly, Pekik Nurwantoro, Gagus Ketut Sunnardianto, Yanoar P. Sarwono, Leong-Chuan Kwek

item.title: QAOA Inside ADMM: Subproblem Wins Do Not Become Decomposition Wins at Matched Budgets
item.description: arXiv:2611.10527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We benchmark the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) as the binary subproblem solver in a two-block alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for mixed-binary problems against classical solvers under matched budgets. With 23 optimizer evaluations per subproblem, scoring determines the comparison: on its final readout, the optimized QAOA loses to random search at $n=12$ and 16 binary variables (inconclusive at 20; exploratory and post hoc tests). When credited with its best sample, it wins. In a noiseless 12-qubit simulation, transferred-angle depth-2 QAOA finds the exact optimum of 97.3\% of planted-family subproblems, against 50.6\%--67.4\% for the four strongest local heuristics (100\% against 90.4\%--94.4\% crediting the four best bitstrings) and a not significantly different 96.5\% for semidefinite rounding with local search (SDP+LS). Under our evaluation-counting convention, its time to solution there is a factor of three to five below the local heuristics' but grows with a larger exponent; it is ten times that of SDP+LS and, in seconds, 54 times that of tabu search with restarts. For the benchmark class, an unconstrained binary quadratic problem in disguise, ADMM's binary step is a proximal step on the reduced problem: at unit penalty ADMM re-solves it, and for larger penalties exact solutions increasingly stall. On two families that do not reduce to one, less accurate solvers found the problem optimum more often at unit and larger penalties. No family gave QAOA a better ADMM outcome than the best classical solver and penalty. The benchmark includes a correctness gate and a log of its hypothesis tests.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Arif Hossain, Sanim Yousuf Fahim

item.title: Beyond the Mean Gap: What Transferred-Angle QAOA Retains on a Superconducting Processor
item.description: arXiv:2611.10529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hardware executions of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are often validated by comparing the device's mean cost with a simulation, a check that can miss what matters for optimization. Under global depolarization, the mean normalized gap and the floor-corrected probability of every set of bitstrings, the optimum included, retain the same fraction of their noiseless improvement over uniform sampling. We test this prediction with depth-2, transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition on the IBM Heron processor \texttt{ibm\_marrakesh}, with and without dynamical decoupling and twirling. At 12 qubits, the main-family circuits retained 29\% to 46\% of their mean-gap improvement but only 5\% to 15\% of their probability of the optimum, lower on at least nine of ten instances per run. Near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum, whereas the avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. In the first submission, a device-matched noise model reproduced the pattern but overestimated the retention of the optimum five- to eightfold. On a rugged planted family, the device found the optimum in 62\% of 768-shot blocks (noiseless: 98\%), within the range of local heuristics. Validations of optimization circuits should report retention of the optimum and of near-optimal sets.
item.dc:creator: Sanim Yousuf Fahim, Mohammad Arif Hossain

item.title: Compact Quantum Channel Attention for Static ASL Recognition: A Controlled Study with Parameter-Matched Baselines
item.description: arXiv:2611.10544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical models often report good accuracy on image tasks, but it is rarely clear whether the quantum part is responsible. This paper proposes QCA-DenseNet, a static American Sign Language (ASL) recognition pipeline in which an eight-qubit variational circuit acts as a channel-attention gate on DenseNet121 features. The quantum channel attention (QCA) gate has 17,464 parameters, 7.51 times fewer than a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) block. The pipeline is tested on 1,815 MU HandImages images by holding out one of five signers at a time, and a frozen-backbone ablation uses small parts of the Kaggle ASL Alphabet data. On unseen signers, QCA-DenseNet reaches 94.50% mean accuracy, above SE (93.72%) and within 0.28 points of the best model. A matched classical MLP and a model without attention perform about the same, and no difference is significant. QCA gives a much smaller attention gate without a detectable loss in accuracy, but no quantum advantage.
item.dc:creator: Ronak Bhalgami, Deep Kothadiya, Nikita Bhatt

item.title: Initialization masks overcome decoding obstructions in compressed QAOA
item.description: arXiv:2611.10588v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In compressed quantum optimization, a variational state is converted into a classical assignment by decoding noncommuting observables. We show that this step creates structural restrictions that changing the initialization can remove, even when increasing circuit depth cannot. For an explicit infinite family of connected cubic graphs on $n=3r$ vertices, with a fixed Pauli encoding and deterministic sign decoder, every all-plus QAOA circuit has cut at most $2r$, at every finite depth and every real angle sequence. A uniform signed product-state mask at fixed depth-one angles has expected cut $13r/4$, an additive advantage $5n/12$; an infinite subfamily admits an optimal mask. A second construction retains a linear depth-one separation under weak weighted couplings, a bounded cost-angle domain and a specified production-encoder ordering. Noiseless simulations then test classical mask selection before energy optimization. On 1,699 random cubic MaxCut instances, one selected mask achieves mean ratio $0.9100$, versus $0.7067$ for the all-plus $X$ baseline and $0.9125$ for the best of $r^2$ separately optimized random masks. On complete cohorts of weighted MaxCut, sparse Ising, Max-2-XOR and Max-2-SAT, the selected mask also improves on the baseline at every size, but it trails the pool at small sizes and leads it significantly only at the larger MaxCut and Ising sizes. Finite-pool order statistics separate the effect of selection from that of drawing a random mask. The results distinguish decoded expressivity from optimized energy and empirical performance; they do not establish a quantum computational advantage.
item.dc:creator: Emilio Semre, Steven Frankel

item.title: Simulating the quantum switch with quantum circuits is impossible
item.description: arXiv:2611.10615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum switch is a higher-order transformation that combines input quantum channels in an indefinite causal order. Whether quantum circuits can simulate its action, and how many calls to the input channels such a simulation requires, are natural questions about the power of quantum control of causal order. In this work, we prove that no quantum circuit with classically controlled causal order can exactly and deterministically simulate the quantum switch for arbitrary input channels using any finite number of calls. This impossibility holds already for qubit channels and extends to the complete $r$-switch, which coherently controls all permutations of $r$ input channels. These results settle the question of exact deterministic circuit simulation of the quantum switch. They demonstrate that processes with indefinite causal order cannot, in general, be efficiently simulated in this setting even by quantum circuits with classically controlled causal order.
item.dc:creator: Caisheng Cheng

item.title: A Grover-Amplified Oracle for Maximum Clique on Graph, Minimum Hitting set and Dualizations on Hypergraphs Built on Quantum Phase Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.10640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we use a quantum circuit called the Graph Encoding Operator which, applied to the complement $\bar G$ of any graph $G$, yields an oracle for the maximum clique problem suitable for amplification via Grover's algorithm. Analogously, we devise a Hypergraph Encoding Operator which, when applied to a hypergraph $\mathcal H$, yields an oracle for the minimum hitting set suitable for amplification via Grover's algorithm. Interestingly, the latter oracle provides, when measured, an approximation of the number of hitting sets of the hypergraph, thus solving the dualization problem for positive Boolean functions represented in a positive irredundant disjunctive normal form. We give the full construction of both operators, prove their correctness, analyze their complexity, and provide an implementation on a quantum simulator. We discuss the resulting complexity, contrast them with existing quantum computer algorithms based on Grover search and we will show that our algorithms outperform, to the best of our knowledge, all of the previous algorithms on space computational complexity by requiring only $O(N)$ number of qubits with respect to the number of vertices $N$, for representing both graphs and hypergraphs in the encoding operator and, consequently, results in an oracle for both graphs and hypergraphs that uses only $O(N)$ qubits even when the hypergraph contains an exponential (on the number of vertices) number of hyperedges.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Pi\~nero, Fernando L. \Pelayo, Hernan I. de la Cruz, Jose J. Paulet, Mauro Mezzini, Fernando Cuartero

item.title: Demonstration of a partial knowledge quantum key distribution protocol
item.description: arXiv:2611.10670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate a novel QKD protocol, named \texttt{Bridge[$d,q$]}, which generalizes the \texttt{SARG04} protocol to $d$ dimensions and $q$ bases. In this protocol, Alice and Bob gain only partial knowledge about each other's raw key. Nevertheless, this partial information is sufficient to distill a definite mutual encryption key. We present an experimental demonstration of the \texttt{Bridge[$2,3$]} protocol. The three unbiased polarization bases were switched using a single Pockels cell. The applied polarization basis switching method is relevant to any 3-basis QKD protocol and to other applications that require fast manipulation of photon polarization qubits.
item.dc:creator: Liran Shirizly, Leonid Vidro, Hagai S. Eisenberg

item.title: From Machine-Discovered Graphs to Analytic NOON State Families
item.description: arXiv:2611.10685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine-discovered graphs generate NOON states after heralding and output-number selection, but their interference mechanisms and optical implementations are not immediately apparent. We derive analytic weight conditions for arbitrary photon number $N$ by counting pair-generation processes that cancel mixed output occupations. These conditions yield quantum experiments by path identity using a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometer and photon-pair sources. Takagi decomposition of the pair-amplitude matrix gives an exact Gaussian implementation using single-mode squeezers followed by a passive interferometer. Any pure, zero-displacement Gaussian scheme with photon-number-resolved heralding requires at least $N-2$ herald photons, and both constructions attain this bound. At finite gain, the ideal Takagi implementation maintains unit fidelity after output-number selection, whereas fidelity decreases in path identity with fixed source settings.
item.dc:creator: Ozra Mahmoudi, Fatemeh Ahmadi, Rahman Nouroozi

item.title: Hidden Coherence and Controlled Quasihole Motion in a Fermionic Laughlin State on a Superconducting Quantum Processor
item.description: arXiv:2611.10687v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states support fractionalized excitations and geometric phases, yet experimentally resolving the many-body coherence encoded in their wave functions remains challenging. Here, we prepare a three-electron $\nu=1/3$ Laughlin state on the Haldane sphere using seven superconducting qubits and reconstruct its many-body density matrix. Through Read's composite-boson construction, we reveal vortex-dressed coherence that remains appreciable over a larger separation range than electron coherence. The extended profile is suppressed in a Fock-diagonal reference constructed from the measured populations, demonstrating its dependence on off-diagonal many-body coherence. We further prepare a one-flux-added quasihole and characterize its fractional charge response against finite-size benchmarks. Controlled quasihole motion yields an effective geometric-phase signature from the reconstructed dominant-eigenstate trajectory. These complementary measurements provide microscopic access to the coherent structure and quasihole response of a finite fermionic Laughlin state, demonstrating an experimental route to probing strongly correlated FQH wave functions on programmable quantum processors.
item.dc:creator: Kui Zhao, Hao Wu, Lei-Yi-Nan Liu, Gui-Han Liang, Cheng-Lin Deng, Cai-Ping Fang, Hao-Tian Liu, Wei-Ping Yuan, Qingyuan Wu, Ziting Wang, Wei-Guo Ma, Hao Li, Jia-Chi Zhang, Tian-Ming Li, Jia-Cheng Song, Zhen-Ting Bao, Zheng-He Liu, Yang He, Yong-Xi Xiao, Yu Liu, Zhongcheng Xiang, Dongning Zheng, Guangming Xue, Haifeng Yu, Kai Xu, Zhao Liu, Kaixuan Huang, Jian Cui, Heng Fan

item.title: Dispersion interaction between two bodies of arbitrary shape
item.description: arXiv:2611.10724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Based on the vacuum tensor Green's functions of electrodynamics, the Lippmann-Schwinger-type equations were derived for the correlations of electromagnetic fields. These correlations were applied within the Maxwell stress tensor and the Lorentz force formula to determine Casimir dispersion forces for two arbitrary bodies. The analysis is performed by the excitation of bodies by electric and magnetic dipoles.
item.dc:creator: Michael V. Davidovich

item.title: Trainability-Simulability Tradeoff in Parameterized IQP-based Reinforcement Learning Policies
item.description: arXiv:2611.10793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameterized instantaneous quantum polynomial-time (IQP) circuits generate distributions conjectured to be hard to sample classically. As reinforcement learning (RL) policies, their $2^n$ measurement outcomes are typically mapped to a smaller action space by a classical decoder. This aggregation can mitigate initialization concentration while making the policy classically simulable. We characterize this tradeoff through the decoder's Fourier--Pauli expansion. Under independent uniform initialization, we express policy variance as an exact sum over groups of nonconstant Pauli components with identical active-generator signatures. Each group contributes its squared aggregate coefficient times $2^{-r}$, where $r$ is the binary rank of its active generators. An inverse-polynomial aggregate coefficient with logarithmic rank prevents exponential policy concentration. Sparse Pauli expansions and contiguous action bins permit efficient classical additive estimation of action probabilities. We introduce a majority decoder combining protected low-weight components with exponentially large exact Fourier support, preserving initialization nonconcentration while excluding polynomial-size enumeration of the exact expansion. Numerical experiments corroborate the variance laws. In ten-qubit CartPole experiments, majority achieves higher returns than recursive parity and the tested local readouts, while higher-weight Pauli sectors contribute an increasing relative share of gradient magnitude during training. A complementary 21-qubit block-chain policy outperforms an extensive pool of fully connected classical neural networks in episode efficiency, even though its bounded-width structure permits efficient classical simulation. These results guide decoder design for quantum and quantum-inspired RL, distinguishing policy nonconcentration, learning performance, and classical simulability.
item.dc:creator: Andr\'e Sequeira

item.title: Trained, Frozen, or Absent: Identifying What a Quantum Layer Contributes to Cross-Sectional Equity Ranking
item.description: arXiv:2611.10801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid quantumclassical models are increasingly proposed for nancial prediction, but reported gains are rarely separated from the classical components around them. We study a hybrid quantum temporal convolutional network for daily cross-sectional ranking of 2000 Tokyo Stock Exchange equities under a protocol built to make the quantum contribution identiable: six conditions (circuit trained, frozen or absent, a parameter-matched classical surrogate, and the circuit alone, trained or frozen) through one code path; four walk-forward folds with ve seeds; bootstrap intervals, Deated Sharpe Ratios, backtest-overtting probabilities and family-wise error control; ve classical baselines including a gradient-boosted tree; and a locked holdout. On 500 out-of-sample days two one-sided tests place the trained-versus-frozen dierence inside 0.03 annualised Sharpe (p = 0.0055, minimum detectable eect 0.02): the circuit is equivalent to a frozen one, not merely indistinguishable from it. With the circuit as the head's only input the two are equivalent inside 0.25; against the network with no circuit the design resolves only 0.50. No condition is distinguishable from zero (best De-ated Sharpe Ratio 0.17). The holdout reproduces the ablation on a protable window, and 2000 US equities reproduce it where every condition loses money.
item.dc:creator: Chi-Sheng Chen, Xinyu Zhang, En-Jui Kuo, Rong Fu, Qiuzhe Xie, Fan Zhang

item.title: MEAT with source and detector correlations
item.description: arXiv:2611.10817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove variants of the marginal-constrained entropy accumulation theorem (MEAT) that enable finite-size security analysis of quantum key distribution with source and detector correlations. For source correlations, our results allow for the state prepared in a given round to depend on the current setting choice and a finite number of preceding choices. For detector correlations, our results require memory effects to persist for a finite number of rounds after a registered click, and all detectors to be switched off during those rounds. These results can be combined, providing, to the best of our knowledge, the first method to jointly treat correlated source and detector imperfections in quantum key distribution. Moreover, we retain all the benefits of the MEAT, such as (but not limited to) support for on-the-fly announcements and choice of adaptive tradeoff functions. The resulting key rates can be computed via a single-round optimization amenable to existing numerical methods. We demonstrate these results on qubit BB84, and exhibit competitive key rates even in the presence of correlated source and detector imperfections.
item.dc:creator: Devashish Tupkary, Amir Arqand

item.title: Periodic Readout Induces a First-Order Generalization Transition in a Quantum Perceptron
item.description: arXiv:2611.10887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational quantum classifiers can generate highly structured decision boundaries through the Fourier dependence of observable expectation values on circuit parameters. We show that expressivity can come at a sharp statistical cost, by considering a quantum perceptron whose readout is the simplest periodic classifier, namely a square-wave function of the weighted inputs, and determine its typical generalization in the thermodynamic limit using a teacher-student replica-symmetric theory. Above a critical oscillation frequency, increasing the training load induces a first-order transition from weakly to strongly teacher-aligned phases, resulting in a discontinuous improvement in generalization. At fixed load, however, increasing the frequency eventually drives the equilibrium generalization error to chance level, despite perfect classification of all the training examples. Thus, the same periodic structure that enhances random-label storage can delay the onset of learning. Our results expose a quantitative tradeoff between memorization and generalization generated purely by periodic readout, and provide a benchmark for understanding Fourier-rich variational quantum classifiers.
item.dc:creator: Fabio Benatti, Masoud Gharahi, Giovanni Gramegna, Stefano Mancini, Vincenzo Parisi

item.title: One Measurement, Many Fronts in Kitaev and Cluster Chains
item.description: arXiv:2611.10912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A projective measurement of one site in the ground state of a quantum chain disturbs the chain in two ways: learning the outcome shifts distant expectation values at once, through ground-state correlations, and the measurement erases the correlations between the measured site and the rest. Both changes travel outward. We solve this problem exactly for the Kitaev chain, the cluster chain in a transverse field, and the Kitaev chain with power-law couplings, and we find that far from the measured site every quadratic observable responds through a front. Where the front is and how fast it broadens depend only on the quasiparticle dispersion. How strong it is depends on two operators: how strongly the measured one creates the fastest quasiparticles and how strongly the observed one detects them; if either factor vanishes, the front is weaker and decays faster. One measurement therefore launches many fronts, one per observable, with a common position and width but different decay laws. In the Kitaev chain the density and the bond energy, the two terms of its nearest-neighbor Hamiltonian, respond to one density measurement with decay laws that trade places between the topological and the trivial phase; in the cluster chain, measuring a symmetry-odd spin instead of a symmetry-even one changes the critical decay law at a fixed Hamiltonian; and with power-law couplings the width law itself changes. All decay laws and profiles are obtained in closed form.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Musat, Stephan Haas, Rishabh Jha

item.title: Bias-free superconducting microwave nonreciprocity from a passive nonlinear resonator
item.description: arXiv:2611.10915v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Routing microwave tones in a nonreciprocal fashion in a superconducting chip usually requires an external bias, commonly in the form of static magnetic fields, pump tones or temporal modulation. Here we demonstrate microwave nonreciprocity in a bias-free, passive platform, a single nonlinear superconducting resonator patterned in one film without Josephson junctions. Unequal coupling with the two feeding ports makes its nonlinear resonance shift direction-dependent, and its sharp Fano lineshape converts this asymmetric response into a large transmission contrast when excited from opposite directions. Our niobium nitride (NbN) device reaches a directional contrast of 53.0 dB at an insertion loss of 4.6 dB, and it exceeds 20 dB over 9.7 MHz. Time-resolved measurements show that the device routes pulses from 2 us to 1 ms with more than 30 dB of contrast and switches within a few microseconds. Made with the same technology as superconducting amplifiers, such bias-free nonreciprocal components could simplify the on-chip routing of strong pump and control tones in quantum processors
item.dc:creator: Brendan MacKay, Abdul Mohamed, Andrea Al\`u, Shabir Barzanjeh

item.title: Deterministically fabricated C-band single-photon sources based on quantum dot circular Bragg grating cavities
item.description: arXiv:2611.10988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Telecom-wavelength quantum light sources are essential components for scalable fiber-based quantum networks, where on-demand emission of single photons is required for high secret key rates. Here, we demonstrate the deterministic integration of metal-organic vapor-phase epitaxy (MOVPE)-grown C-band InAs/InP quantum dots into circular Bragg grating resonators. The integrated emitters exhibit a radiative lifetime of $T_1 = (1400 \pm 50)~\mathrm{ps}$ and a spectral linewidth of $\Delta E_{\mathrm{FWHM}} = (41.0 \pm 4.0)~\mu\mathrm{eV}$. Under non-resonant excitation, we measure a post-selected single-photon purity of $(0.95 \pm 0.02)$ and a raw two-photon interference visibility of $V_{12\mathrm{ns}} = (35 \pm 2)\%$, which increases to $(70 \pm 18)\%$ under temporal post-selection. We discuss strategies to improve photon indistinguishability, including radiative-rate engineering, charge stabilization, and more selective excitation. Our results combine MOVPE growth, deterministic device integration, and telecom C-band emission, providing a route toward scalable semiconductor quantum light sources for fiber-based quantum networks.
item.dc:creator: Monica Pengerla, Yury Berdnikov, Alexander Kosarev, Dominik M. Feder, Avijit Barua, Aris Koulas-Simos, Pawe{\l} Holewa, Sven Rodt, Imad Limame, Elizaveta Semenova, Stephan Reitzenstein

item.title: A Witness for Quantum Correlations Using Nonlinear Spectroscopy
item.description: arXiv:2611.11021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ability to detect and quantify entanglement in molecular systems is essential for understanding their quantum correlations and to evaluating molecules as platforms for quantum technologies. Here we show how signals from existing spectroscopic techniques can provide sufficient information to witness entanglement. The main ingredient is a spectroscopic map from admissible quantum states to a finite-dimensional space of signal coefficients, which are expectation values of state-independent effective observables. The molecular response model and measurement protocol determine the effective observables for a fixed system bipartition, and the spectroscopic map defines sets of joint expectation values compatible with all admissible quantum states and their separable subset. We illustrate the construction of the effective observables and their expectation value sets using rotational invariants and the spectral structure of optical signals. Fluorescence dynamics and photon coincidences provide a complementary example. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for entanglement certification with established spectroscopic techniques.
item.dc:creator: Julia Liebert, Gregory D. Scholes

item.title: Exact sampling beyond Fock inputs and linear optics: photon-number superpositions, photonic matrix-product states, adaptive and non-linear circuits
item.description: arXiv:2611.11044v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clifford and Clifford's algorithm samples single-photon boson sampling exactly, one output mode at a time, by adding the input photons in a uniformly random order. We extend this construction to other input states and to adaptive and non-linear circuits. It applies whenever non-negative weights on output prefixes and input sets satisfy one marginal identity, a set-chain lemma: the random-order sampler is then exact at one weight evaluation per candidate mode, and it gives the posterior over the hidden input set. We build four exact samplers on it. For sources in a superposition of vacuum and one photon, the weights are rectangular permanents on an offset input set, and the cost has the exponent of single photons under loss. For photonic matrix-product states of bond dimension $\chi$, a gap-by-gap Kraus contraction turns each weight into a short sum of squared amplitudes. For adaptive linear optics, the chain starts from the posterior given the adaptive counts and rejects chains that contradict them. For a single-mode non-linear phase the identity fails, and rejection from linear branches is exact with acceptance $1/\|c\|_1^2$. All four samplers agree with strong simulation on small instances, and cost models put adaptive sampling with up to three adaptive modes within $10\%$ of single photons and a non-linear site at $\varphi=\pi/2$ at about $4\times$.
item.dc:creator: Jean Senellart, Stephen Wein, Pierre-Emmanuel Emeriau

item.title: Bridging Gaps with Tensor Networks: From the Haldane Gap and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2611.11049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proofs generated by large language models are often difficult to understand, generalize, or formalize directly. Here we verify, digest, and formalize OpenAI's computer-assisted proof of a uniform gap in the periodic spin-1 Heisenberg chain using tensor-network diagrams and Lean 4. Reading the partition-function network along space and imaginary time shows how finite-ring bounds propagate across doubled lengths and inverse temperatures to all longer even rings, sharpening the spin-1 bound from the same finite inputs by a factor of 19 to $\Delta_L > 0.0729$ for all even $L \geq 36$. We identify reflection positivity as the general condition behind the proof and certify uniform gaps in seven additional spin chains and ladders. More broadly, digesting machine-generated proofs into transparent physical mechanisms yields sharper bounds, broader theorems, and reusable formal verifications.
item.dc:creator: Sirui Lu

item.title: Towards large-scale ab initio Molecular Dynamics Simulation with Efficient Sampling-based Quantum Computing Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2611.11084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) requires the calculation of highly accurate electronic-structure energies and nuclear forces at every time step, which can quickly become computationally expensive. Sample-based quantum diagonalization offers a route to such calculations on quantum hardware, but its use in AIMD simulations has so far been limited to active spaces of about 20 qubits. In these spaces, exact diagonalization is tractable, and the quantum circuits are typically built from standard coupled-cluster amplitudes. Here, we introduce SqDRIFT-AIMD, which combines randomized sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SqDRIFT) with analytical nuclear gradients. With SqDRIFT-AIMD, we obtain more accurate ground-state energies than the conventional coupled-cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) driven AIMD simulation for the $40$-qubit active space. We apply SqDRIFT-AIMD to study the dynamics of proton transfer in the Zundel cation, using circuits executed on IBM Heron r3 quantum processors. SqDRIFT energies fall below CCSD across the $40$-qubit double-well PES and stay within a few m$E_\text{h}$ of CCSD at 52 qubits. The $40$-qubit SqDRIFT-AIMD trajectory tracks the SHCI-driven proton transfer to within $1.33$ m\r{A} and exhibits excellent total energy conservation, with a standard deviation of only $0.245$ m$E_\text{h}$. These results extend quantum-centric AIMD to active spaces beyond the reach of exact diagonalization.
item.dc:creator: Ankit Khandelwal, Nirmal M R, Aaryav Mishra, Debasmita Bhoumik, Dhinakaran Vinayagamurthy, M Girish Chandra

item.title: Adaptive Quantum Metrology of Gravitational Waves
item.description: arXiv:2611.11157v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a feedback-controlled quantum metrology scheme to probe weak gravitational waves (GWs) through their direct energy exchange with light. Adaptive SU(2) direction control, based on current estimates of the GW frequency and phase, allows the frequency shifts acquired in successive interaction intervals to add rather than cancel. The resulting persistent frequency difference is converted into an optical phase difference for interferometric readout. We further extend the scheme to elliptically polarized GWs using two transverse sensing channels separated by $45^\circ$ to probe the $+$ and $\times$ components independently. After the GW interaction, the two signals are mapped onto orthogonal polarization modes, enabling phase accumulation along a common path. We derive the corresponding quantum Fisher information matrix and find a $T_{\rm int}^2T_{\rm ph}^2$ scaling in the ideal coherent regime. For a fixed-photon-number probe, the sensitivity shows Heisenberg-like $1/n$ scaling in the ideal case.
item.dc:creator: Wan-Ting He, Shuang-Quan Ma, Ke-Mi Xu

item.title: Quantum entanglement as a resource for self-organization and stabilization
item.description: arXiv:2611.11175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can quantum entanglement generate macroscopic order that persists after the entanglement itself disappears? We establish such a mechanism in a driven-dissipative bosonic lattice, where local entanglement enables transport that amplifies spatial fluctuations into extended Turing patterns. For the full nonlinear dynamics with noise and disorder, we derive rigorous finite-time bounds on pattern intensity for all admissible separable evolutions, allowing arbitrary classical correlations. Quantum dynamics produces pattern intensities beyond these bounds during both formation and stabilization under noise. The excess intensity also provides a lower bound on the accumulated transport contribution beyond the separable limit. We further introduce an environment that responds to emerging order by suppressing local coherence and activating classical transport. The patterns then persist as local entanglement is lost, with both stages arising from a single time-independent Lindblad equation. These results show how transient quantum resources can establish persistent macroscopic order, opening new directions for harnessing self-organization in nonequilibrium systems.
item.dc:creator: Kazuki Ikeda

item.title: Hardware-Efficient Continuous-Variable Quantum Computation: Finite-$N$ Non-Gaussian Gates in a Floquet-Engineered Cavity-BEC
item.description: arXiv:2611.11245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous-variable (CV) quantum computation in bosonic modes offers a hardware-efficient route toward fault tolerance, yet synthesizing deterministic, macroscopic non-Gaussian gates with Wigner negativity remains challenging. Here, we establish two physical breakthroughs and two tensor-network innovations using a single-cavity 87Rb Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) as a macroscopic bosonic logical mode. Physically, building on our orthogonal optical dual-driving architecture, we propose deterministic, unitary Floquet-engineered Two-Axis Twisting (TAT) non-Gaussian gates without post-selection, and introduce a paradigm shift from quantum metrology to CV quantum computation: via a normal-ordered Holstein-Primakoff expansion and non-perturbative spin simulations, we show that the over-squeezed regime ($t>t_{opt}$, where Wineland squeezing $\xi_R^2$ degrades) harnesses finite-$N$ Bloch-sphere curvature - manifesting at $O(1/S)$ as cubic shearing and quartic Kerr $(a^\dagger a)^2$ interactions - to deterministically generate Wigner negativity. Methodologically, we formulate an exact automaton Matrix Product Operator in the compact SU(2) spin basis with an $N$-independent Liouvillian bond dimension ($D_L=6$), bypassing Fock cutoff errors ($N_{max}$) and $O(N^3)$ permutational-invariant scaling. Finally, we decouple $4^N$-dimensional Lindblad evolution from collective observation via an Exact Bilateral Dynamic Programming Dicke Projector with log-gamma normalization, extracting the $(N+1)\times(N+1)$ symmetric projection $\tilde{\rho}_{n_L,n_R}$ without moment truncation while tracking symmetry retention $p_{sym}(t)$. Our proof-of-principle $N=50$ benchmark resolves deep Wigner negativity ($W_{min} \approx -0.214$ at $t=2.00\mu$s, after $\xi_R^2 \approx 0.124$ at $t_{opt} \approx 0.64\mu$s), establishing a scalable architecture for $N \sim 10^3-10^5$ macroscopic BEC processors.
item.dc:creator: Soi-Chan Lei

item.title: Unbounded advantage of adaptivity in entanglement-assisted communication
item.description: arXiv:2611.11333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Shared entanglement can reduce the amount of classical communication needed to perform distributed computation. This can be achieved either by first measuring the entanglement and then communicating classically, or by adapting the quantum measurement to the received message. Here, we introduce tasks that adaptive protocols can solve using just three entanglement-assisted messages, while the communication cost grows without bound when the quantum receiver is not adaptive. Consequently, no bounded amount of classical communication can reproduce all correlations generated by an entanglement-assisted ternary classical channel. We establish two complementary limitations on the relation between adaptive and non-adaptive quantum protocols. First, every adaptive protocol using a finite entanglement dimension admits a non-adaptive simulation at finite communication cost. Second, every adaptive protocol sending $d$ messages can be simulated to within error $\varepsilon$ using $O(d\log(1/\varepsilon))$ non-adaptive messages. Our results reveal the fundamentally unbounded advantage of adaptivity in quantum communication, but also that observing very large advantages requires both high-dimensional entanglement and very precise observations.
item.dc:creator: Armin Tavakoli

item.title: What an Observer Reads off a Holographic Screen
item.description: arXiv:2611.11356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What does an observer read off a holographic screen that is an array of qubits rather than a surface? In the generalized holographic principle the interaction between two separable systems acts on such a screen as a weighted sum, up to an overall prefactor, of commuting observables with values plus and minus one. When the weights are nonnegative and the prefactor is one and the joint eigenspaces are lines, everything a probe reads off the spectrum depends only on the list of weights, which we call the profile. On the screen with equal weights summing to one the running dimension read by a diffusion probe falls short of two at unit time by at most twice the reciprocal of the number of qubits; a geometric profile gives instead, through its level count, a plateau of any positive height. An observer correlates sets of qubits; its readout carries a profile at a given weighting when the levels it reads, counted with multiplicity, are those of a screen with one weight per set. We prove that a readout carries a profile at every weighting exactly when the distinct nonzero traces of its qubits are linearly independent over the field with two elements, the trace of a qubit being the list of sets that contain it; such a readout is a partition of the qubits it covers up to an invertible recoding, and a dependent one carries a profile only on finitely many proper linear subspaces of weightings. Refining a grouping without end builds a tower whose boundary is a profinite set and hence a condensed set, on which a strictly positive compatible profile separates the locally constant functions by a distance. Applications certify probabilistic and strong contextuality and give the leading shortfall of the distance between the poles of the fuzzy sphere; in a model of monogamous entanglement the pairs that weight-one threads representing operational ER=EPR can occupy at once are exactly the partial matchings.
item.dc:creator: Kenan Oggad, James F. Glazebrook, Chris Fields

item.title: Information--control limits for record-indistinguishable reset of a monitored qubit
item.description: arXiv:2611.11393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A qubit that is continuously monitored from the moment it is prepared in its excited state writes evidence of that preparation into its measurement record. We ask how much control is needed to reset such a qubit to its ground state while keeping its complete record statistically close to the record of an undriven ground-state qubit. The qubit is measured in $\sigma_z$ at rate $\Gamma_m$ with efficiency $\eta$ and has no relaxation. For feedback that acts causally on the record, distinguishability is the Kullback--Leibler divergence $D$ of the controlled record law from the reference law, and the control cost is the quadratic effort $J$, the integrated squared Rabi frequency. We prove that every open-loop drive leaves $D$ infinite and that every admissible control obeys $DJ\ge\Gamma_mU(\eta,D/\kappa_0)$, where $U$ is given by a one-parameter family of integrals and $\kappa_0=1-\ln2$. Our main result is the exact high-effort constant $\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\inf\{DJ/\Gamma_m: D\le\epsilon\}=K(\eta)$, where $K(\eta)=[\int_0^\pi\sqrt{2\eta(1+\cos\theta)^2+(1-\eta)\sin^2\theta}\,d\theta]^2$; an explicit sequence of two-phase feedback policies attains it. The first term of the integrand is the population evidence that the record receives while the qubit is rotated toward the ground state. The second is the price of the impurity created when the unrecorded part of the measurement dephases the coherence that the rotation needs; the record receives this evidence later, when the measurement repurifies the qubit. The global constant $c(\eta)=\inf DJ/\Gamma_m$ satisfies $K/2\le F_2\le c\le K$, where $F_2$ is again given by an integral; $c$ is known exactly at $\eta=1$ and in the limit $\eta\to0$. With any nonzero relaxation rate the unconstrained infimum of $DJ$ vanishes, so $c(\eta)$ is specific to the relaxation-free model.
item.dc:creator: Sinan Bugu

item.title: High-Dimensional Maximally Entangled OAM States by Joint Pump and Modal-Space Engineering
item.description: arXiv:2611.11395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) generates correlated photon pairs that inherently exhibit high-dimensional spatial entanglement in orbital angular momentum (OAM) modes. In practice, the resulting two-photon states are typically not maximally entangled due to a highly non-uniform distribution of generated OAM modes. Although pump-beam engineering has emerged as a tool to prepare high-dimensional entangled states, it has usually been restricted to low-dimensional subspaces, i.e., small sets of selected OAM modes for each photon within the full infinite-dimensional two-photon Hilbert space. A general understanding of the requirements for the generation of maximally entangled states (MESs) for any dimensionality $d$ with $d>2$ is lacking. Here, we demonstrate how pump engineering enables the generation of high-dimensional MESs for arbitrary $d$ defined in $d \times d$ subspaces. By identifying the interplay between the spatial pump structure and the choice of OAM subspace, the required pump profile for a target MES is directly determined. Our results reveal that maximal entanglement with OAM requires a careful and nontrivial design of the effective high-dimensional Hilbert subspace.
item.dc:creator: Richard Bernecker, Baghdasar Baghdasaryan, Fabian Steinlechner, Stephan Fritzsche

item.title: Universal robust nonadiabatic geometric quantum computation with shortened composite pulses on superconducting circuits
item.description: arXiv:2611.11420v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The nonadiabatic geometric quantum computation (NGQC) using the nonadiabatic geometric phases is a promising strategy to realize the high-fidelity quantum operation for large-scale quantum processing. However, conventional NQGC schemes combining with optimal control techniques to further improve the gate fidelity and robustness usually either comes at the cost of prolonged gate time or require complex pulse control and only are limited to several certain specific quantum gates or/and for a certain type error source. Thus, implementing universal and robust geometric gates with simple control while further suppressing gate times remains a major challenge. Here, we propose a scheme for universal robust geometric gates with shortened composite pulses, where the pulse control is simple and enough available evolution parameters can be utilized to effectively reduce the sensitivity to universal systematic errors. Numerical simulations demonstrate that our universal geometric gates set exhibit much stronger error resilience than their conventional single-loop counterparts. Finally, we also verify the robustness advantage of our scheme on realistic superconducting quantum circuits with experimentally demonstrated technology. Therefore, our work paves an alternative way to achieve high-fidelity and robust geometric quantum computation against multiple errors.
item.dc:creator: Cheng-Yun Ding, Na Kuang, Yu Jin, Li Tang, Rui Huang, Li-Hua Zhang

item.title: Alchemically Transferable Parameters for Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
item.description: arXiv:2611.11445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine-learned circuit parameters could remove one of the main bottlenecks of variational quantum eigensolvers: the classical optimization loop, with its typical barren plateaus, local minima, and costly energy and gradient evaluations, is replaced by a direct prediction. Prior work showed that machine-learning models paired with a structured circuit design can transfer across system size and structure within hydrogenic systems. The next step: Extending them to organic molecules would seem to require re-training on use-case-specific training sets. In this work, we show that this is not necessary by establishing an alchemical approach. A geometric projection places surrogate hydrogen atoms along the bond directions of the target molecule and so maps its local bonding environment onto small hydrogenic fragments. Existing hydrogenic solvers can then be reused as they are. The only new quantity is a single projection radius per bond type, which is fitted once on a small reference molecule and reused unchanged thereafter. We demonstrate the approach on the separable-pair circuit designs that have been used in prior work and extend the approach to multi-circuit approaches that span effective bases for quantum subspaces.
item.dc:creator: Jonas Motyl, Jakob S. Kottmann

item.title: One Bit, Many Records: Information Replication in Quantum Many-Body Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.11446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Information replication occurs when a single locally encoded classical bit becomes simultaneously readable across extensively many disjoint regions of a quantum many-body system. Here we identify dynamical selection as a mechanism for generating these records, whereby an unperturbed nonthermal reference remains locally recognizable while its locally perturbed counterpart spreads and relaxes under the same Hamiltonian. We establish an entropy-capacity criterion showing that a uniform area-law reference paired with a volume-law perturbed branch guarantees extensive records at a fixed, nonzero information threshold. An embedded-dimer chain demonstrates both record proliferation and increasing readout reliability with fragment size, while stabilized PXP dynamics extends the mechanism to a coherently recurrent reference. These results characterize information spreading through the spatial multiplicity of accessible records and provide experimental signatures measurable via fixed local readouts.
item.dc:creator: Dan-Bo Zhang, Yan-Ming Chen

item.title: Quantum State Reconstruction from Sklar-Type Relational Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.11468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sklar's theorem in classical probability theory rigorously separates the marginal statistics of a joint probability distribution from its dependence structure data. We apply this perspective to the context-dependent classical probability tables induced by the Born rule for a quantum state. For each Born probability table of a given quantum state, we discard the marginal statistics of the individual parties, retaining only the relational data among them. Yet we prove that, when these classical relational data are collected over all contexts, the nontrivial quantum compatibility constraints inherent in quantum mechanics suffice to reconstruct any irreducible multiqubit quantum state itself. This means that the local information of the subsystems, discarded table by table, is fully recovered. We call this quantum-state reconstruction from Sklar-type relational data.
item.dc:creator: Yi-Yu Lin, Jie-Chen Jin

item.title: Weight-Space Programming of Variational Quantum Circuits: Large Language Models Write Quantum Circuit Parameters Without an Optimizer
item.description: arXiv:2611.11537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) optimize circuit angles through repeated quantum-device evaluations, often facing vanishing gradients and high optimization costs. We ask whether a large language model (LLM) can write these angles directly. Extending *weight-space programming* from classical networks to quantum circuits, we provide a frontier LLM (\gpt) with the problem, circuit, and gate conventions. Its angles are executed exactly as written, without returning losses, gradients, or accuracy feedback. Across 139 requests, we test handwritten-digit classification, VQE ground-state estimation for spin chains and H$_2$, and MaxCut QAOA, comparing against random weights, classical optimization, and optimization initialized with LLM weights on the same circuit. When parameters have interpretable structure, the LLM matches or approaches the optimizer: it achieves 95--100\% of the energy spectrum on every VQE problem, derives the exact H$_2$ ground state in closed form, finds optimal depth-one QAOA angles for every graph, and reaches 93--96\% accuracy on digits 3 versus 8 with 12--18 hand-written weights, outperforming an optimizer trained on the same ten examples. Its weights are also strong warm starts: optimization reaches its best value after a median of one evaluation rather than hundreds. Allowed to design circuits, the LLM chooses data-dependent rotation chains encoding pixel importance in all 30 cases (one qubit for binary tasks, one chain per qubit for ten classes), reaching 65\% accuracy across ten digits. Yet the approach fails in opaque weight spaces: accuracy drops to chance when fixed circuits exceed 30 weights, while optimization improves. It is also sensitive to gate conventions: 6 of 42 QAOA replies reverse mixing-angle signs and fail. We release all prompts, replies, and scores.
item.dc:creator: Debarshi Kundu, Swaroop Ghosh, Vasant G Honavar

item.title: A Microscopic Model Underpinning Macroscopic QED in Active Media
item.description: arXiv:2611.11557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a microscopic foundation for macroscopic quantum electrodynamics in active media. Starting from a driven three-level system, we derive an effective two-level description with nonequilibrium stationary populations and employ a quantum central limit approach to obtain collective Langevin dynamics. This construction yields the electromagnetic susceptibility and quantum noise-current correlations from the same microscopic stationary state, providing a direct connection to the reservoir operators of conventional macroscopic quantum electrodynamics. We show that the optical response is governed by the population difference, whereas the noise correlations depend separately on the populations of the two levels. Consequently, at optical transparency, the imaginary part of the susceptibility vanishes while quantum fluctuations remain finite. We interpret the resulting noise statistics in terms of an effective reservoir occupation and a purification involving two vacuum modes, and establish a corresponding effective-temperature fluctuation--dissipation relation. Finally, we demonstrate that the residual fluctuations at transparency can induce finite heating of a nearby quantum probe.
item.dc:creator: Daigo Oue

item.title: A geometrical approach for obtaining exact analytical solutions for a scalar field in a one-dimensional dynamical cavity
item.description: arXiv:2611.11595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The dynamical Casimir effect was first predicted by G. T. Moore in 1969, who considered a real scalar field inside a cavity with a moving mirror in ($1+1$)D, satisfying Dirichlet boundary conditions. Moore wrote the general solution for the field in terms of a function that satisfies a functional equation nowadays known as the Moore equation.In the literature, exact analytical solutions to the Moore equation form a rather small set, restricted to specific classes of laws of motion. Cole and Schieve (1995) developed a geometrical approach that yielded a general formula for the solution of the Moore equation for cavities initially at rest. However, its application has always been done through numerical calculations, and their approach has therefore long been regarded solely as a numerical method. In this work, we show that their method can also be employed as a powerful method for deriving exact analytical solutions, and show the applicability of this approach to deriving analytical solutions to the Moore equation. We obtain original exact analytical solutions for an expanding cavity with a uniformly moving mirror, a contracting cavity with a mirror that approaches the static one asymptotically, and, in addition, we recover the first analytical solution to the Moore equation for a resonant mirror motion, originally obtained by Law in 1994. Moreover, we extend the Cole-Schieve approach, showing that exact solutions can be constructed from any spacetime region where the Moore function has already been determined. We show that this extended geometrical approach allows us to expand the set of known analytical solutions to the Moore equation from the few classes of motion reported in the literature to an infinite set, as it enables the treatment of new classes of laws of motion obtained by combining those presented here with each other as well as with previously known classes of trajectories.
item.dc:creator: Maxwell F. de Ara\'{u}jo, Odemar Juli\~{a}o do N. Neto, Stanley S. Coelho, Jeferson Danilo L. Silva, Alessandra N. Braga, Danilo T. Alves

item.title: Proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture: An Exposition
item.description: arXiv:2611.11626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an exposition of a recent proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, which states that every degree-$d$ polynomial $p : \{0,1\}^n \to [0,1]$ has a variable of influence at least $\mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{Var}(p)/d)$. This implies that quantum query algorithms for decision problems can be efficiently simulated classically on most inputs. It also yields a near-equivalence between the status of the $\mathsf{BPP}$ vs. $\mathsf{BQP}$ problem in the random oracle and unrelativized worlds. We organize the proof around four main steps and discuss how each connects to the literature on the analysis of boolean functions and probabilistic combinatorics. To bring out the key ideas, we do not optimize parameters, and our presentation yields weaker exponents than the original. $\textbf{Authors' note.}$ The proof was discovered by David Turturean using a research system developed at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), in combination with a non-public Anthropic model. The proof was then shared with the authors, who worked to understand it and prepare this exposition. Anthropic's public models were used in this process. The authors did not receive financial compensation from Anthropic or PSI. This article is not intended for publication at a conference or in a journal.
item.dc:creator: Guy Blanc, Jordan Docter, Carmen Strassle, Li-Yang Tan

item.title: Pauli propagation in adaptive local frames
item.description: arXiv:2611.11647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The cost of Pauli propagation depends on the local basis in which the evolving operator is expanded. We show that its Pauli complexity splits into an occupation part, invariant under local rotations and bounded from below by the operator mass and length distributions, and a flavour part that a suitable basis can remove. We introduce frame-adaptive Pauli propagation (FAPP), which rotates the basis of every qubit, gate by gate, to the principal axes of the operator's local polarisation, exactly and within the memory structure of Pauli propagation. This simple rule achieves most of what the best local frame can, and the polarisation predicts how much any local frame can gain. In the Ising chain in transverse and longitudinal fields, FAPP lowers the truncation error at fixed memory by up to an order of magnitude and the memory by a size-independent factor of three; on the infinite two-dimensional lattice it needs up to seven times fewer strings for a given certified accuracy, and in Clifford circuits doped with T gates two to eight times fewer.
item.dc:creator: Jonnathan Pineda-Jim\'enez, Mario Collura

item.title: Model-family selection and recovery-gate design in generator-based noise tomography
item.description: arXiv:2611.11748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Family selection in generator-model noise tomography, usually quoted as a property of the hardware, is a hypothesis test whose shot floor is closed form, $N^{*}=\lambda_{\mathrm{req}}/(r_{\mathrm{b}} S)^{2}$, controlled by the absolute bias $r_{\mathrm{b}} S$ rather than by the relative residual $r_{\mathrm{b}}$, and therefore computable for any device before a single shot is taken. The same computation prices the recovery gates, because the fingerprint that fixes a family's residual and the Fisher information that ranks the designs are read off the same map: there is no design-independent verdict and no family-independent design optimum. Whether a design can move that price is structural, not numerical: a bias confined to the block every design measures identically is design-blind, while one that reaches the code blocks can be repriced by a factor of sixty-eight. The two platforms here are its extremes, at $98.1\%$ and $48.0\%$ in the design-blind block. At the reference point the floor is $1.1\times10^{7}$ and $6.7\times10^{6}$ shots per component for the two families, so at the $10^{5}$ shots a run spends the test has power $0.053$ at a level of $0.05$ and the residual it reports is shot noise. Rebuilding the fingerprint under each of the sixty-four designs moves the floor by $68$ on one platform and $1.7$ on the other, and the most precise design costs ten times more shots for the verdict than the cheapest to test. All sixty-four placements are full rank, so the design problem is one of conditioning: at three gates the rms varies by factors of $2.7$ and $3.9$ with placement alone, while the optimum over counts is flat. At five qubits the same rule moves the floor by $21$, while the verdict itself costs $10^{9}$ shots; checked against the calibration of a real three-qubit register, the floor is a requirement on systematic control before it is a shot count.
item.dc:creator: Long Huang

item.title: Advantage Distillation in Paired-State Quantum Key Distribution
item.description: arXiv:2611.11754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate advantage distillation for paired-state Loop-Back quantum key distribution, with a fixed optical station serving a lightweight portable terminal. Alice prepares two polarization-encoded pulses, Bob selects and applies a polarization filter to each pulse, and Alice infers his selections from the returned detection pattern. The proposed advantage-distillation step selects consistent blocks of three two-bit records using two independent public parity checks on a minimal connected graph. The closing edge of a parity polygon is shown to be redundant: any spanning tree of the same vertices has the same acceptance set. We derive exact acceptance probabilities, residual-error laws, and retention rates. Under independent bit errors, the three-record filter reduces the leading error term from e to e^2, while its cost in discarded records and public information is accounted for explicitly. A modular security theorem bounds the additional guessing advantage available to an adversary after syndrome disclosure and block acceptance, including arbitrary quantum side information. We also evaluate a specified single-photon passive-tap optical channel, obtaining a positive conditional entropy bound and exact accepted-block security quantities.
